strengths: The central empirical finding is clear and useful: averaged activation differences on unrelated text expose narrow finetuning objectives through token decoding and steering. This provides a practical diagnostic and a meaningful caution for interpretability benchmarks built from model organisms.

The evaluation covers 33 organisms across four training families and seven models spanning 1B–32B parameters. Position analyses, base-to-finetuned-chat comparisons, full-finetuning experiments, and alternative agent models provide substantial evidence beyond isolated demonstrations.

The automated auditing results show a large practical improvement: ADL-assisted agents reportedly identify broad objectives in 91% of cases versus 39% for the strongest black-box baseline. Strong performance without additional interactions supports the informativeness of the supplied activation analyses.

The intervention and data-mixing experiments go beyond descriptive correlations. Particularly valuable is Appendix D.4, where mixing reduces readable traces while emergent misalignment persists, partially separating the interpretability artifact from the underlying behavior.
weaknesses: The claim that these findings establish a fundamental limitation of model organisms as realistic proxies is stronger than the evidence. Recovering the final narrow objective when comparing against a pretrained model does not establish that it completely overpowers chat-training information. The realistic-domain extension contains only three vision-language finetunes, and its text-only interaction restriction limits conclusions.

Comparisons do not establish ADL's advantage over alternative model-diffing approaches. The cited logit-difference amplification method is an especially relevant missing baseline. Agent ablations separating steering, Patchscope, and Logit Lens are also absent. Moreover, interaction budgets exclude substantial ADL preprocessing and cached generations, so the results demonstrate information utility rather than matched-cost auditing efficiency.

The causal intervention establishes that the direction contributes to domain modeling, but does not uniquely identify overfitting: an appropriate domain prior could produce the same opposing effects on domain and general-text loss. Gemma's pretraining loss worsens after intervention, and there is no held-out generalization analysis establishing overfitting in the conventional sense.

Evaluation depends heavily on LLM-selected scales, LLM relevance judgments, and LLM hypothesis grading without reported human calibration. Maximum-over-position relevance is an optimistic summary, and different organism-specific rubrics make pooled grades and threshold-based success rates difficult to interpret uniformly. Repeated agent runs help, but do not resolve systematic grading bias.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The manuscript omits important training settings, including learning rates, training duration, batch sizes, and LoRA configuration; mixing experiments also lack sufficient detail to assess exposure and optimization controls. Model identities alternate between Llama 3.2 1B and 8B, and captions and prose disagree on whether some experiments average three or five SDF organisms.

strengths: The paper establishes a useful empirical finding: average activation differences on unrelated text can expose narrow finetuning objectives. Combining these differences with existing decoding and steering tools provides a simple, meaningful baseline for model-diffing research.

The main evaluation covers 33 model organisms, four organism families, and seven models spanning 1B–32B parameters. Additional experiments examine full finetuning versus LoRA, extraction positions, alternative agent models, and comparisons against pretrained rather than chat checkpoints.

The agent evaluation supplies concrete evidence beyond selected qualitative examples. ADL-assisted agents reportedly identify broad objectives in 91% of cases versus 39% for the strongest blackbox baseline, with five repeated runs per configuration.

The intervention and data-mixing experiments strengthen the descriptive findings. Particularly valuable is Appendix D.4, where mixing reduces readable traces while emergent misalignment persists, helping distinguish detectability from the underlying behavior.
weaknesses: The strongest conclusions exceed the evidence. Detecting a narrow objective in a base-to-finetuned comparison does not establish that it 'completely overpower[s]' chat-training information or that model organisms are generally unrealistic. The domain-adapted multimodal experiments provide some external validation, but their text-only interaction restriction limits the comparison.

The causal experiments establish that the identified direction affects training-domain and pretraining losses; they do not uniquely establish overfitting. A useful domain-prior shift could produce the same pattern. Held-out in-domain losses, general capability measurements, and comparisons at matched target-task performance would better distinguish specialization, forgetting, and pathological overfitting. Gemma also contradicts the predicted pretraining-loss improvement.

Comparisons do not isolate ADL's contribution sufficiently. The paper cites logit-difference amplification but does not compare against it, and the agent evaluation lacks steering-only, Patchscope-only, and Logit-Lens-only ablations. Random-direction controls are provided for causal interventions, but analogous controls for the extraction pipeline would strengthen attribution. The interaction budgets also exclude substantial ADL preprocessing, so they do not establish equal-cost superiority.

Evaluation depends heavily on unvalidated LLM judgments. Token relevance reports the maximum over positions using knowledge of the true domain, making it an optimistic diagnostic rather than a deployable selection criterion. The organism-specific grading rubrics measure different levels of specificity, and the headline greater-than-30-fold improvement relies on a roughly 1% baseline. Human calibration and uncertainty intervals for these success rates are needed.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The manuscript omits important training settings such as learning rates, training duration, batch sizes, and LoRA configurations, and does not sufficiently specify the hierarchical statistical model. It also inconsistently names Llama 3.2 as 1B versus 8B and describes some experiments as averaging over three versus five SDF organisms. These ambiguities complicate independent verification.

strengths: The central empirical finding is compelling: mean activation differences on unrelated text reveal narrow finetuning objectives across 33 organisms, four organism families, and seven models spanning 1B–32B parameters. This is a useful contribution to model diffing and interpretability evaluation.

The agent evaluation provides concrete evidence of practical utility beyond selected qualitative examples. ADL-enabled agents identify broad objectives in 91% of cases versus 39% for the strongest blackbox baseline; repeated runs and alternative agent models strengthen this result.

Several complementary experiments support the phenomenon: token decoding, steering, positional analysis, full versus LoRA finetuning, and comparisons against pretrained rather than immediate pre-finetuning checkpoints.

The mitigation experiments are informative. Mixing unrelated data reduces readable traces while largely preserving false-fact alignment in some models; the additional emergent-misalignment experiments show that behavioral changes can persist despite reduced detectability.
weaknesses: The interpretation as overfitting, and especially the conclusion that these organisms are fundamentally unrealistic, exceeds the evidence. Increasing finetuning loss while decreasing unrelated-data loss under ablation demonstrates a distributional trade-off, but does not distinguish overfitting from useful domain specialization. Gemma also contradicts the predicted unrelated-data effect. Detecting narrow training through a base-to-finetuned comparison does not establish that it completely overpowers chat-training representations.

The comparative evaluation does not isolate which ADL components matter. There are no agent ablations separating Patchscope, Logit Lens, and steering, nor comparisons against the cited logit-difference amplification approach. The blackbox comparison demonstrates informational value, but its interaction budgets exclude ADL's substantial activation collection and steering calibration costs.

Quantitative conclusions depend heavily on unvalidated LLM judgments. Human calibration of relevance and hypothesis grades is absent, and the organism-specific rubrics differ substantially in difficulty and specificity. Consequently, the headline improvement in identifying 'specific details' is difficult to interpret uniformly. Maximum-over-position relevance scores also provide an optimistic summary rather than typical extraction performance.

The broader applicability remains uncertain. Twenty of the 33 organisms are SDF variants, subliminal learning has only one example, and the causal analysis focuses on small SDF models. The realistic domain-adaptation extension shows much weaker signals, while its text-only interaction restriction limits conclusions about multimodal auditing.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Important training settings, including learning rates, training duration, and LoRA configuration, are not specified. Several passages identify Llama 3.2 as 8B while figures identify 1B, and descriptions disagree about whether causal and mixing results aggregate three or five SDF organisms.
